Photograph: Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty Images US-Israel war on Iran Iran targets US bases as Israel warns sanctions could drive Tehran to ‘desperate steps’ Air bases used by US in UAE and Kuwait hit as Israeli defence chief says Iran’s regime fears collapse due to economic pressures Peter Beaumont Senior international correspondent Thu 3 Sep 2026 10.16 EDT Last modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 11.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Iran has continued to demonstrate an ability to target bases in the Gulf used by the US despite six months of war and a new sanctions regime described by the Trump administration as an “economic D-day”. As Iran’s military targeted US bases in the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait, despite threats of further strikes by the US president, Israel’s defence chief warned that economic pressures from the sanctions could lead Tehran to escalate to more “extreme measures”. “This morning, the army hit the satellite communication systems, equipment depots and fighter aircraft hangars of the terrorist US army at the Ahmad al-Jaber air base in Kuwait with missiles and drones,” the Iranian military said on Thursday in a statement carried by state television. The “location of forces and radar systems of the child-killing US army at the Al Minhad air base in the UAE were also attacked by missiles and drones of the army”, it added. In a post on X, Kuwait’s ministry of defence said its air defences had intercepted missile and drone attacks during a “blatant Iranian aggression”. The Kuwaiti statement came after the US allies Bahrain and Jordan said their air defence systems intercepted several Iranian air attacks on Wednesday. Fighting between the US and Iran has increased this week after the US hit Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz on Sunday, claiming that Iran was planning to use them to shoot mines into the waterway. View image in fullscreen Damage to a residential building after an Iranian drone attack, according to Kuwaiti authorities, in Kuwait City on Thursday. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images The latest flare-up in the conflict comes amid little evidence that the Trump administration is succeeding in advancing its nebulous war aims either on the battlefield or via mediation, despite the US president’s repeated claims to have opened the strait of Hormuz to oil traffic. Instead, traffic through the key maritime passageway remains far below prewar levels, with oil prices remaining stubbornly elevated ahead of US midterm elections. Oil prices jumped again on Thursday after the Iranian strikes. Among the weapons Iran has used this week is its Kheibar Shekan medium-range ballistic missile system. The cheap and accurate missile can be launched within minutes and has become a staple of Iranian strikes. The rocket’s solid fuel motor means it does not require lengthy fuelling. It can be deployed very quickly to avoid detection and can be armed with a powered and steerable final stage to help beat anti-missile systems. Despite claims by the Trump administration that Tehran is running out of rockets, Iran continues to fire missiles that are considerably cheaper to produce than the US interceptors used to shoot them down. Iran has claimed as recently as the end of August that it maintained both missiles stockpiles and the ability to manufacture them. “Initially, some believed that Iran had only a limited number of missiles and that its stockpiles would eventually be depleted as the war continued,” the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesperson Brig Gen Hossein Mohebbi said. “However, that assumption proved incorrect, as Iran’s missile capability has remained sustained and its missile production has continued.” Mohebbi’s characterisation of Iranian missile stockpiles could not be verified. The continued strikes came as Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, said that while the new US economic sanctions appeared to be effective, the increased pressure could lead Tehran into extreme measures. “We see signs indicating that the heavy economic pressure they are under, and the fear of an uprising and the collapse of the regime, may push them to desperate steps,” Katz said at a ceremony for defence ministry employees. The hawkish minister reiterated the threats against the Islamic Republic that he has made in recent months. “An Iranian attack on Israel will free Israel from any existing constraint,” he said. “We will strike all of Iran’s national military and civilian infrastructure – including energy infrastructure – and push Iran deep back into the stone age.” Explore more on these topics US-Israel war on Iran Iran Strait of Hormuz US foreign policy Middle East and north Africa Donald Trump Israel news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Iran accuses US of ‘war crime’ after missile blast kills four people at wedding ‘It’s a fever dream right now’: sailors of USS Abraham Lincoln voice joy after arriving in Thailand Trump threatens further action as US and Iran exchange fire in new flare-up First US military attacks on Iran in a month prompt retaliation US threatens severe sanctions against countries with economic ties to Iran Iran vows to retaliate against countries that cooperate with fresh US sanctions Iran’s foreign minister calls threat of new US economic sanctions ‘desperate’ Trump demands Iran pay compensation for decades of US soldier deaths Netanyahu rejects US-led 15-point Gaza peace plan in rare public break with Trump Travelling through Iran reveals mixed narratives about the US-Israel war Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

She said the ASD did not know how many agents were on the internet: I think that prospect of getting some sort of definition or calculation of how these agents are out there is really remote, and I would just say a lot. She said Australian systems faced “enormous” hidden costs of maintaining outdated technology but said they needed to be addressed: If we don’t move fast enough, almost certainly it would be legacy technology which is first compromised in a major AI-enabled attack.
